Among the Tyrannidae, the White-winged black tyrant (Knipolegus aterrimus) exhibits a life history shaped by the thermal conditions of its montane habitats. In southern populations, newly laid eggs weigh approximately 2.95 grams [Ww0 = approximately 2.95 grams], a surprisingly modest initial mass derived from eggs averaging 22 millimeters in length and 16 millimeters in width. This frugal starting investment contrasts with the considerably larger ultimate wet weight for females. Adult females achieve a maximum body mass of 20.2 grams [Wwi = 20.2 grams], a size typical of insectivorous flycatchers that must balance the energetic demands of aerial foraging with the costs of reproduction. Comparative data from related Knipolegus species suggest that this lean body plan is an adaptation to life in open, windswept elevations where prey availability is seasonally pulsed and predictable.

Respirometry trials conducted on active individuals under controlled laboratory conditions provide key insights into the species' metabolic physiology. Measurements taken at a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] revealed a maximum basal metabolic rate of 56.36 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 56.36 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This comparatively elevated metabolic rate likely reflects the high costs of sustained flight and thermoregulation in a cool, high-altitude environment. When compared to other tyrannids of equivalent adult body mass, the White-winged black tyrant appears to maintain a metabolic scope that supports its active, sallying foraging strategy. The correlation between body mass and oxygen consumption in this species underscores the tight energetic coupling between somatic maintenance and locomotor demands, a pattern frequently documented in Neotropical passerines occupying similar ecological niches.

The timing of early developmental events in Knipolegus aterrimus is closely tied to incubation temperature. Under stable incubation maintained at 37 °C [T = 37 °C], the incubation period culminates in hatching after 15 days [ab = 15 days], a duration that aligns with the altricial developmental mode common among suboscine passerines. Once hatched, the nestling phase proceeds rapidly under the same thermal conditions that characterize the active adult metabolic state. At a consistent environmental temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the young birds achieve fledging at 14 days after hatching [tx = 14 days after hatching], a remarkably short nestling period that reflects intense parental brooding and frequent provisioning visits. This accelerated developmental trajectory may represent an adaptive response to high predation pressure, minimizing the window of vulnerability for the nest-dependent chick during its most exposed life stage.

Sexual maturation and the onset of reproductive capability follow a distinct timeline in this species. The period from hatching to puberty spans 39 days [tp = 39 days] when individuals are maintained at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a relatively rapid gonadal maturation for a bird of this body size. However, the transition to actual first breeding is deferred considerably beyond the attainment of physiological maturity. The time since birth at first brood is approximately 438 days [tR = approximately 438 days] under the same thermal regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This substantial lag between achieving puberty and initiating reproduction is consistent with a life-history strategy in which young birds delay breeding until they have acquired sufficient foraging experience and established a territory. Such a pattern is common among long-lived tropical and subtropical passerines that face strong competition for limited nesting resources.

Reproductive output and survivorship schedules complete the demographic profile of the White-winged black tyrant. Females typically produce 2 to 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 to 3 eggs per clutch], with a single clutch laid each year [F_R_i = single clutch laid each year], generating a modest annual reproductive rate that prioritizes offspring quality over quantity. Under the prevailing conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the maximum lifespan recorded for this species reaches approximately 9 years [am = approximately 9 years], a longevity that distinguishes it from short-lived northern temperate tyrannids. This extended lifespan, combined with delayed first reproduction and low annual fecundity, places Knipolegus aterrimus firmly within the slow end of the life-history continuum among Neotropical flycatchers, where adult survival is at a premium and reproductive effort is carefully hedged against environmental unpredictability.
